reference.source: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)
clinicalPearls: Assess and resuscitate simultaneously using the primary survey sequence: airway with cervical spine protection, breathing, circulation with haemorrhage control, disability, and exposure with environment control
Life threats identified during the primary survey are treated as they are found, before moving to the next step
The most common preventable cause of early death is uncontrolled haemorrhage, so external bleeding is compressed and internal sources are sought promptly
Permissive hypotension and balanced resuscitation with blood products help avoid dilutional coagulopathy in bleeding patients until definitive control is achieved
The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy worsens outcomes and guides damage-control strategies
A structured secondary survey (head-to-toe examination and history) is performed only once the patient is stabilised, to detect injuries missed initially
Reassess frequently, as trauma physiology is dynamic and deterioration can be rapid
Adjuncts such as focused ultrasound, chest and pelvic imaging, and blood gases are integrated into the primary survey
reference.pathophysiology: Polytrauma involves injury to two or more body regions or systems, at least one of which is life-threatening. Simultaneous tissue damage triggers haemorrhage, hypovolaemic shock, and a systemic inflammatory response. Hypoperfusion causes tissue hypoxia and lactic acidosis, while ongoing bleeding and crystalloid dilution impair clotting. Hypothermia further inhibits enzymatic coagulation, and the resulting lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy establishes a self-reinforcing cycle. Later, immune activation predisposes to systemic inflammatory response syndrome, acute respiratory distress, and multi-organ dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated major haemorrhage from a single cavity (chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones)
Neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury
Cardiac tamponade or tension pneumothorax as the cause of shock
Medical collapse (e.g. cardiac event, seizure) preceding a traumatic mechanism
Toxicological or metabolic contribution to altered consciousness
additionalInvestigations: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST/eFAST) to detect free fluid and pneumothorax
Chest and pelvic radiographs as primary-survey adjuncts
Whole-body CT (trauma pan-scan) in the stabilised patient to map injuries
Arterial blood gas with lactate and base deficit to gauge shock severity
Group and crossmatch, coagulation studies, and viscoelastic testing to guide transfusion
redFlags: Persistent or recurrent hypotension despite resuscitation, indicating ongoing haemorrhage requiring immediate surgical or interventional control
Rising lactate or worsening base deficit signalling inadequate perfusion
Signs of the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) mandating damage-control resuscitation
Deteriorating conscious level suggesting evolving brain injury or shock
Mechanism or examination suggesting occult truncal or pelvic bleeding
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on injury burden, time to haemorrhage control, and physiological reserve. Early definitive control of bleeding and correction of the lethal triad improve survival, whereas prolonged shock and multi-organ dysfunction carry high mortality.
pitfalls: Completing the secondary survey before life threats in the primary survey are addressed
Over-resuscitation with crystalloid worsening dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia
Anchoring on an obvious dramatic injury while missing a silent source of shock
Failing to reassess after each intervention as physiology evolves
Neglecting active warming and haemostatic resuscitation in the bleeding patient
management: Simultaneous assessment and resuscitation by the primary survey sequence, treating life threats to airway, breathing and circulation as they are found with cervical spine protection
Immediate control of catastrophic external haemorrhage and prompt identification of internal bleeding, with damage-control surgery to arrest it
Damage-control resuscitation using balanced blood-product transfusion, permissive hypotension and early tranexamic acid until bleeding is controlled
Aggressive correction of the lethal triad by active rewarming, restoring perfusion to reverse acidosis and correcting coagulopathy guided by viscoelastic testing
Structured secondary survey once stabilised to detect missed injuries, followed by definitive fracture fixation and organ repair
Critical care support for shock, acute respiratory distress and multi-organ dysfunction
Early rehabilitation and multidisciplinary trauma team coordination across the surgical specialties
